📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Modernising Retail at Scale: Architecting a Cloud‑to‑Edge Platform for a Global Enterprise.

Industry observers note that jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce.

Jayesh Bhayani is Senior Engineering Director at Tesco, playing a central role in leading technology strategy and shaping business direction. His work focuses on creating strategic clarity, architectural direction, and organizational alignment needed for the business to compete at pace in an increasingly disruptive retail environment, driving enterprise scale and agentic commerce readiness.

Recent findings suggest that software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

It has been revealed that jayesh Bhayani: I'm going to spend some time in sharing our learnings of transformation at scale at Tesco. That's why modernizing technology at Tesco. How it has changed the culture, not just within the company, along with systems, but enabled the growth for the company. From that perspective, after 10 years being at Tesco, I thought it would be good to share the learnings we had from here and how we are looking at the future.

I was in California, in Silicon Valley, for about 25 years, when Tesco reached out to me, saying, would you like to work at Tesco? I had got no concept of Tesco, because I had never come to London before that. When I looked at the website, it was a pretty basic website. The outside-in perspective, when you look at the website of a large grocery chain, feels like there is no technology. This went on for a few months. After that, they convinced me to talk to a few people in the technology department. The state that this technology was, and what was needed for growth and the transformation that was needed at scale, was what motivated me and my wife. We were empty nesters already by that time. We decided, why not? Came here. Just around that time, Trump got elected. We felt even better.

First of all, some context into how large Tesco is. There are about 5,000 stores. Some of them are super. Some of them are medium. Some of them are small. They are across five different countries. We used to be in Asia as well, when I started 10 years back, in Thailand, Malaysia. We divested those businesses. We are still in five countries. We have 20 distribution centers. We have 25 million customers. That's almost one-third of the UK population. That's not small. We have 350,000 colleagues across our stores. Out of that, maybe around 15,000 in head office. Out of that, around 6,000 in technology. Again, it's big. It's big operations, large number of colleagues. We do around 50 million baskets. Not number of transactions, the baskets, which means the orders across our estate in our stores. We do 1.3 million online orders in a week. When COVID came, many companies talk about scale.

When COVID happened, when entire business shifted towards online, our challenge was to double the number of online slots that we can make available for our customers. By that time, for the e-commerce part, our platform was already live. When we doubled it, that's equivalent of putting almost three other competitor companies online in one month. Many companies stopped taking orders. Many companies stopped signing customers. We doubled it in a month. That again shows the scale. Fifty million cases through supply chain, huge. We are not even talking about number of miles the trucks travel and the logistics within the distribution center. We do 4.5 billion calls a day. We have 98% UK coverage when I talk about 25 million customers, but coverage-wise in terms of online business, that can cover the entire geography of UK. We cover almost 98%, which means you can have your home delivery of grocery done in 98% of the UK.

In a recent development, tills, as we call it here in the UK, POS systems, as called in many other countries, almost 50,000. That's just POS devices. We are not talking about all other thousands and tens of thousands of handheld devices that run on the same platform. That's just the context, because that sets a very different tone for the kind of technology, how mission-critical technology becomes. Then driving transformation through that is quite challenging, because I worked at startups. I've worked at mid-size companies. I had my own startup. Being in California and not having a startup is a crime. I tried that, too. I worked at Yahoo for 10 years. I worked at large companies, worked at startups. Tesco is yet another scale. I wanted to reflect here, because it drives quite a lot of complexities in decision-making of what would you do with your transformation and technology choices.

In a recent development, this goes beyond retail. Any industry that has got physical estate, digital, and real-time operations will face these complexities. That's where we learned about being both efficient and effective. Efficient is do things well, fast. Effective, do good things, which are more effective. A slight difference in nuances. You can be doing fast all the things, but if those are not the right things, you are chasing wrong goals. Do the right things and do things the right way, efficiency and effectiveness. I wanted to share here, this is not just about retail. This will apply to many of the industries who operate at that kind of scale and complexity.

Industry observers note that let's start as to why. Ten years back, why did we need transformation? It was quite a poor state within technology I'm talking. When they talked about a large grocery organization and I was thinking there is no technology inside, there was a lot of technology, but it was very siloed. Multiple technology stacks tied to historical business structures. When I'm talking siloed, this is not just, store had a POS system and e-commerce had something else. I'm talking multiple stacks within online or e-commerce business itself. Grocery, its entire stack. We had marketplace back then, completely different stack. One Microsoft, .NET, one Oracle. F&F, our clothing, Tesco wine. Customers across these, forget having single account, did not even have single login. Jayesh@groceryhomeshopping is different than Jayesh@marketplace, is different than Jayesh@f&f. We had no single customer view, no data platforms, no product management, nothing. It was that fragmented. There was no single identity, as I just explained.

Industry observers note that no single source of truth for stock or pricing. From that perspective, when you have multiple monolithic systems running in private data centers, we were not in public cloud back then. It was not even private data cloud. It was just a bunch of machines. You would be lucky if you asked for a server and you get a server in two months. That was the state. Decades old POS system, 20 years old software running on our POS systems in the stores, completely batch oriented. You couldn't connect to them. The deployments were the engineers would go with the floppy disk and then will deploy the software in the stores. Third-party solutions, not just third-party solutions, they were heavily customized, because when you are at the scale of Tesco, you can demand saying, I need a slightly different thing in your software. Sounds good initially. Then you're locked in with a very customized version of vendor solution for multiple years.

It has been revealed that we had software running from vendor solutions that were at least a decade old. You can't even upgrade them. Then heavily outsourced resources as well. These were where we had lots of consulting firms providing resources for us. Not a good culture, not good quality. You can imagine what the landscape was when we started 10 years back. At the scale of Tesco, that becomes quite complex to say, how do you find your journey through that?

It has been revealed that that got us the imperative for change, saying we definitely need omnichannel experience, because customer expectations were moving very fast. The old style of doing business was not working. Technology was not helping business. Business had all the motivation to change. Technology was stuck. We had hit the wall, literally. Global coherence across physical and digital estate, both. Rapid change cycles. Back then, as I noted, if you talked to a vendor and asked for a solution in our POS systems, it would be six months for minor changes. Regression on top of that, so three things would be broken. You do the testing, and they charge you for fixing the bugs again. It would be six to nine months before you could get anything out on our Tills or POS systems in stores. Forget e-commerce. Then along with that, of course, we needed higher reliability, higher capability. We needed omnichannel experience, higher security, everything.

In a recent development, it needed more capability and capacity, both. That led to us chasing from fragmented stacks to unified platforms that could serve all our channels across all our markets and develop a multi-tenant platform. That's what we developed. It was called only platform. Sometimes platform terms are confusing. I'm not talking just the tech platform. I'm talking about the retail platform that runs our business. We'll talk about tech platform as well. That's part of our learning as to how tech platforms are super important if you don't start early. When we started, it was a retail platform to say, how do we now enable all these businesses and develop the retail platform?

Where are we now? All of our entire UK business and Republic of Ireland business runs on this platform, 100%. We are making inroads in our Central European businesses. There are multiple countries there. They all have their nuances. The trust in technology is much higher. Technology strategy is very well integrated with the business strategy. It's not like service-oriented mindset of say, we just need three things. Go ahead and can you build it? That's how the siloed happened long time back. We'll talk about that in our transformation journey. As I remarked, the platform is much more scalable but also capable. That's where we are now. We'll talk about how we are looking into the future of agentic commerce from that perspective. Technology has become an integral part of the entire business ecosystem. It's no longer a separate unit that sits in a corner and gets three orders to say, can you develop this for us?

This I describe in my own language. Let's now talk about the journey of transformation. Most companies most people assume that when you talk about transformation, you're talking about system transformation, which is, develop the platforms. We'll talk more about that. That's what I talked about until now. That's not enough. What we had to do along with that was talent transformation. Was very service-oriented mindset, as I mentioned. Most of the development was outsourced. We had to completely change our career paths, the titles within that, the job definitions within that, and completely transform the talent internally. When you want to insource that, that's a huge task. Back then we were only across two different locations, UK and India. As part of this transformation, we started two more, Hungary and Poland, because we had to scale and we needed good talent. The combination of that was required. As I mentioned, the career frameworks were redefined across product, engineering, and program.

In a recent development, product did not exist. Product management did not exist back then. It was only program and mostly service engineering. The right org structure is super important as part of that as well. You can have talent, but if they're not set up in the right organization, it does not work. It generally should map the business domains and the business structure. For example, in Tesco, there are four major business units, supply chain and distribution, commercial unit where you decide as to, should we sell potatoes and tomatoes that leads to almost a ranging of 40,000, 100,000 SKUs saying what are we going to sell across our estate? What should be the price of that? What should be the cost of that? What kind of promotion should we run? What kind of store design should be there? How many aisles should be there? Which product goes in which aisle? That's completely very complex business.

That's all trading decisions. Channels, which is where online and stores where customers actually buy things. Then customer area, which is mostly loyalty programs and stuff like that. We had to mimic that within technology to say we are going to completely map ourselves into how the company is laid out. You can't run your own ship in a large company and say that we are just different. That doesn't work. Because if you're not sustainable, transformation will not work. That's talent transformation, and we had to change recruitment processes well along with that. The third pillar of this one was process transformation. You can have the right talent, you have the right motivation because you need good challenges for right talent, which is system transformation. If your processes are not conducive, then that fails. The reason why we had silos, not that anything is wrong with program management. We still have hundreds of program managers, but the role of program manager was very different.

In a recent development, some business person would have a favorite person in technology, as I said, it was a phone call away. No one knew about technology. They will talk to a program person and say, can you get this done? They will run around, talk to a bunch of service engineers, outsource it, comes back a solution. The silo gets deeper and deeper and deeper. We had to establish that from program led, we are going to be an agile product-driven firm. We develop products, not just solutions. We'll talk more about some of these, mostly in the systems area. I'll refer to a couple other things as needed, because today is just a teaser of the transformation. I'm trying to compress 10 years of our learnings.

That led to, in the system transformation, what's the strategic framework? One of the very early things we had to decide was build and buy. Build versus buy, many people call it, we call it build and buy. Why? Because while we wanted to insource and build the platform internally with insource resources, you will need to buy many technologies along with that. What we noted was, we'll always tend towards building things which are core differentiator for our business. That's how we will win. Something that is not a core differentiator, we'll just buy. Most of the enabling function, as we call it internally, which is back-office applications like people system, finance system, everything, they're not a core differentiator. The retail platform is a core differentiator, including the POS system that runs on every single Tills. You go to Tesco, that's our homegrown system. When you use your scan-as-you-shop device, some of you might be shopping in Tesco, you use those handheld devices, completely synced, runs on the same platform.

Every single device runs on our platform. Cameras runs on our platform. Everything runs on our platform. Those are the core differentiator. Where we buy, platform integration is a must. That's how we say. Platform and domain boundaries. Now, centralization versus decentralization. The reason why I mentioned this here is if you're going through this space, and now even more so, 10 years on it's a different world with the agentic workforce that's coming. You can't centralize things. Gone are the days of change control board, architectural board, queue up in front of those pedestals and get your design reviewed and get your code reviewed and everything. We had to decentralize that. That's where we had to come up with very clear domain boundaries, good set of standards. Freedom within the guardrail, that's how we call it. Freedom within the framework with those guardrails to say how are we going to do it, and then you can decentralize that.

It has been revealed that tech excellence. Tech excellence is not just tech debt. We call it tech excellence, because it's proactive as well. It is not just, do we have a few bugs that we need to do? Or, do we need to patch our operating systems? Of course, yes. How are you taking care that you're not going to face into those challenges on an ongoing basis? Back then, there was no concept of total loss recovery. How do you blueprint for total loss recovery? This is not DR. DR is basic. When you're talking about total loss recovery, it's a completely different ballgame. The kinds of capabilities you need for that, we start to put that into tech excellence. Because it's very easily assumed, even within technology, and I'm not talking outside technology. Of course, business teams don't have that level of understanding. Even within technology, anyone who is not in engineering will assume that this gets done by some engineers who had a good coffee on a good day on the side of their desk.

It doesn't happen that way. You have to dedicate time for that. You have to dedicate focus for that. That requires education. Outside engineering, that requires education. Outside technology, as well, at some point. Where now our business leaders talk about tech excellence saying, are you sure it's built right? It's needed. That's the cultural change we are talking about. That creates the framework for a much faster pace of delivery and clear ownership, as I said, with the clear domain boundaries, and strong and long-term resilience.

That strategic framework gave us, what are the core tenets of our platform? Only customer is not enough. Yes, we are driven by customer. That drives our business. If you only think about customers, that's not enough. For the size of Tesco, when you've got almost half a million people working for you, colleague experience is equally needed. All the systems that we run in our stores, the operational systems that we run for our business operations, everything needed to be transformed, not just the customer-facing applications. Partners, we had very poor rating from our suppliers back then. We had to establish the trust, but also build the systems to make sure that our suppliers, partners, people who give us potatoes and tomatoes to sell for grocery, I'm referring to those partners, not tech partners, we had to improve experience for that. Reuse across multiple different markets and business units.

Industry observers note that offline operations. When you are talking about thousands of edge devices working in your stores, one of the most critical requirements for us is a network can be flaky. Because if you get in the business of replacing network of your entire thing, you might be spending hundreds of millions. Grocery is a very low margin business, it's around 4%. Some are 3%, some are 4%, some are 4.5%. It's a very low margin business. Every penny that you spend counts, goes in your P&L. Cyber risk and compliance built-in into the platform. Super important. This is where we had to innovate across all three public clouds. We did create private cloud, not just a server sitting in our data centers, and edge platform as well. As I was just referring to low margin business, cost is a feature for us, not a constraint. We don't see cost as a constraint.

Industry observers note that it's a very different mindset. As part of one of our learnings, we'll go through the learnings, but since we are talking about that, when we jumped into public cloud, and this now will apply into agentic code development as well, and we are thinking through that. The value that gets created against the cost that you might be spending, you've got to be very careful about that. We were spending upwards of £50 million, £60 million on public cloud. I'm talking four, five years back. It was growing exponentially. If you don't control that, then you've got £50 billion business, which was back then, with 4% margin, you're talking about £2 billion. When you talk £100 million of just cloud cost, I'm not talking our salaries, I'm not talking about entire technology department, this is just cloud cost. You can imagine how much P&L you are impacting at that level. It's the responsibility of the technology department to say, how do you keep cost as a feature, not as a constraint?

Industry observers note that then we came up with good principles for our platform, which, as I stated, domain design was very important. Create composable services. Data pathways and data quality both matter. You need very clear data pathways as to how data would flow between the various different operating datasets to data lakes, but also data quality across each one of these steps. Security in a layered defense model, all the way from perimeter to built inside. We got tons of different layers of how do you think about security. Multi-tenancy by default, which is, you build the platform once. Even from the physical deployment perspective is the same deployment that works and enables multiple countries for us, multiple different businesses. Build product capabilities, not just solutions, not point solutions. Build products, build capabilities. Then abstractions, all of you will understand that. It's not just for hiding complexity but also when you got mobile applications running across thousands of microservices, running in the data center or in the cloud.

For example, add an item to your shopping cart has got at least 40 different microservices called. Get the identity token, get the product ID, get the customer UUID, get their personalization preferences, get the price, check all that, get the product description. After that, it goes in the basket. Now if you are not creating abstractions that's going all the way from someone's mobile phone all the way to your data center or public cloud, and adding an item if it takes 40 network round trips, you are extremely slow. Yes, it is of course for hiding complexity, but at this scale all that matters. That's what went into our principles because that created cohesion across, as I was saying, digital and physical estate without becoming bottleneck.

That was one of the lessons learned to say, while you are trying to do that, sometimes it's good to build more centralized capabilities first before you jump into that. It takes a little longer but saves you costly migration. From that perspective, any services that needs true elasticity and scalability we put it in public cloud. Public cloud is a dual-edged sword because when you start using PaaS, Platform as a Service, you get very tightly bound to that public cloud because many of them are very proprietary services. You will never get out of that. You lose your flexibility. As Tesco, at our scale, we like that flexibility. Whether it is when we buy the technologies for our use, deployed or in the cloud, anywhere, we care a lot about saying, does it give us flexibility or not? Because if you're not careful, the license fees keep on increasing exponentially.

If you are locked in, it's a very well-known fact that you will be held hostage. If you don't use PaaS then it's just a compute environment. Why are you in public cloud in the first place? You see, it works both ways. What we try to use is all portable PaaS technologies within the public cloud, that gives us that freedom. It's not perfect. I will not claim that. That does give us an optionality when it's needed. Then, many of our large systems, we are talking about supply chain systems, distribution centers, technologies related to that, we tend to run that into our private cloud. It's almost 80-20, 80% of our presence is in private cloud, 20% is in public cloud. Cost-wise, exact flip of that, 80% of the cost is in public cloud, 20% of the cost is in private cloud. It costs almost 8 to 10 times more for an equivalent setup in public cloud.

Recent findings suggest that this is where as we are talking about agentic code development and everything, a developer could spend almost £500 a day without realizing or without clarity on what value is getting created. Again, if you step back historically this is where public cloud was almost 10 years back. Easy to jump in, hard to explain what value is getting created. The learnings here that we are talking while the technology will keep on evolving is pretty much where you can reapply.

Then comes the edge part of it. As I was saying, when you are at the scale and you want omni-channel experience, how do I now create a platform that is going to power your edge as well? What we did was, the same platform services, the microservices that run in our cloud, they run in our scaled environment with the right abstractions in our edge devices as well. There is a real consistency of business logic. There is a real consistency from data perspective, because when the network is there it's constantly exchanging data. For whatever reason, if the network is not available, we are able to identify the customer. If you have a club card, we identify your loyalty. We fail in favor of our customer. Let's say you did disable your club card literally last minute and network is chopped off and you are in the store, yes of course, that's a real-time requirement, but we fail in favor of our customers.

We take the payment, not cash, credit card as well. Very lately we have enabled contactless payment as well. That's a huge set of capabilities. It's pretty much, you don't realize the store is running offline. The pricing on the shelf edge, that has to be considered. Now as many companies are talking about electronic shelf edge labels, that's part of our consideration in the platform, saying, what happens when the network is not running. How would you revision prices on the shelf edge labels? All this gets very taken for granted. Even I wasn't aware as to what's the level of complexity when you are in a retail business with hundreds of thousands of such devices running across thousands of stores. One part which we made sure was, it's the same team which is responsible for edge platform as well as our retail platform in the cloud. That made sure that consistency was there, that ownership was there.

Industry observers note that in fact, when we were migrating from legacy stack and we were transforming, we made sure it's the same team that owned the legacy platform as well. You cannot compartmentalize and outsource the problem even within the technology department, saying, A team is building fresh services and A team will take care of the old services. Never works. You lose motivation very promptly.

Industry observers note that this is where we were talking about workload placement. We touched upon this a little bit before, which is, a single team owns that thing. We do use portable PaaS technologies when we are using the public cloud. In public cloud, we generally favor the systems that need scale and they are closer to the customer from that perspective. We, for the private environment in data centers, enabled the cloud as well so that for the developers it's the same experience when you are in the private cloud. We centralized a lot of our shared services. What initially started as, and this is probably a misconception, me being in technology, I'm 35 years in technology, that engineers love doing all these things. Setting up your Cassandra's, setting up your Kafka's, figuring out all the protocols. Yes, all that is true in the beginning part of the transformation. As we started putting more and more production workloads, because early on as part of our talent transformation we decided there is no separate QA team, there is no separate support team.

Sources indicate that of course, first-line support is different, but then pretty soon the call does come to our engineers so they are fully responsible for support of production environment. What started as a good challenge, as a good hobby, learning new technologies, pretty soon became very onerous. When I talk about creating shared services, so I own the retail platform, I own the tech platform, we'll talk about tech platform at Tesco, and I own the applications as well. It's not as much fun for engineers today to say, I'm going to deploy my own Cassandra, I will do the partitioning, and I will do all these things. It gets very onerous at some point. We invested a lot in shared services to say, how do you now not worry about all these things?

In a recent development, the sequence is very crucial. When we started 10 years back, and we are talking about a tech giant which is 100-plus years old, when we were talking about product development, the misconception in the business teams was, prepared meals in a box is called product. That was the journey when we started. When we started talking about platforms, we had to choose our sequence in the right way. You can never do Massive Bang. You cannot ask a 50 billion business to stop and pause and say, we will come back in two years or one year or three years and we'll change everything. Even within that staggered approach, that you see from 2016, this is the real chart. In fact, we stopped counting at 2024, and we had only put significant items here. We had to pick our sequence. Initially it was very far and few in between. We had to develop and create that trust in technology from the business side to say, how are we going to figure this journey out.

It has been revealed that there was a lot of distrust when we started. You have to find the right demand, where the business demand, the customer demand is there, and find the right opportunities to do transformation in small steps early on, and then it gets bigger and bigger. Now we get more demand from the business with more trust, less questions. You say, how can we do it right?

In a recent development, we have been using AI for a very long time at Tesco. That's nothing fresh for us. For example, start with all those business units I was saying, supply chain. One of the biggest challenges is forecasting how much customers would buy. If you go wrong in that one, it either leads to loss in millions or very poor customer experience. For example, if you forecast that you will sell 100kgs of tomatoes. It's in tons generally. I'm just taking an easy number. Except if you go wrong, either your shelves will be empty because customers are buying more and you need more than 100kg, or you will end up buying too much and it goes to waste. Waste is a big number. We try to control that, and we have done very well on that one. That's a tiny example, but that whole forecasting is dependent upon what's the lead time to getting the products.

In a recent development, like tomatoes can be supplied four times in a day in our distribution center. Something like jeans might be six months in advance. Then the shelf life could be very different. Tomatoes will get rotten in few days, non-perishable items will stay on the shelf for longer time, so the combination of that. That's the supply chain side. Distribution, how are you going to lay out all that stock? What's the stock management? What's the truck routing algorithms? Because we are talking about hundreds and thousands of miles of trucks traveling every day. How are you going to optimize that? Good for environment, good for company, good for everyone. How do you fill the truck? This is just touching into the supply chain area. Likewise, when you talk about ranging, you talk about customer experience in personalization, you talk about pricing, everything is AI driven. How are we thinking about agentic commerce?

Because that changes the paradigm completely. What I remarked is agentic commerce is a business decision. Because if you don't participate in agentic commerce, you can be marginalized. Because, let's say most customers are spending time on ChatGPTs and Geminis of the world, and they are going into agentic commerce to say, we can do grocery for you. Of course, they want that. Nothing wrong in it. That's where customers are. If you don't go there, you can be marginalized. If you go there, you can still be marginalized because you're losing the first touch, customer experience. Because now you outsource that experience to someone else. Hence, it's a business decision. It's not just a technology decision. Getting ready requires complete shift. How would you be ready for agentic commerce? Because what used to be the simple SEO and SEM, the metadata and data on your website where the search engines will come and crawl your website and then you appear in the searches, organic search or paid search.

According to recent reports, now the agentic crawlers will come and you need much more machine-readable format of that data so that agents can understand. That's just the AEO, agentic understanding. We'll look at the architecture as to how you will prepare for that kind of integration. You will need the same kind of identity consent and policy frameworks as to how much you can allow the agents to operate on your website or through your APIs. Then multiple protocol interfaces are emerging, UCPs, ACPs. The platform completely evolves from a system of record, that's how it used to be, to a system of delegation. Because now those agents are working with your data, with your services, making decisions for the customer. It's a complete delegation.

That's the harness, how we are thinking. We are still going to use the platform because the core capabilities are still within our retail platform. If you look at the bottom left, customers, the bottom part is the existing path, existing online channels or stores from that perspective, existing application gateway, existing experience APIs going into our platform, retail platform. When you're talking about the agents on the top, you'll need now the gateways for the agents. How would you allow them? How much would you allow them? Which one would you allow them? The commerce protocol, ACP and UCP, now there are severe regulations in the UK for making payments, not allowed for agents to make payments on behalf of customers. Again, there are differences between the countries and regions to say what is allowed, what is not allowed. Many of these technologies, and I'm talking about both UCP, ACP, we are in direct conversation, are not ready for production scale yet.

Sources indicate that as much as there is marketing, they are not ready. For Tesco scale, again you need very different readiness. We are not even talking about risk and compliance and anything here. I'm just talking pure technology risk here. Then you will have your own sub-agents that might be running, which might be talking to these agents and hence agent-to-agent protocol. You will need MCP for discovery of many of these services, discovery of data. Many of our application experience APIs were built for the applications that we built, like add item to basket, for example. You might need those plus some more for the agentic experience, but going back into the same retail platform. That's how we are looking into the future and thinking how we are going to do that.

Sources indicate that what could have been better is, build central tech platform early. As I mentioned, we jumped in early into the public cloud and then we realized that everyone had their own version of CI/CD platforms and observability and everything. Now when I was talking to my own teams, say, we got best CI/CD pipelines, and every team was saying that. I don't need 50 CI/CD pipelines, I need one CI/CD pipeline. Portfolio management, we introduced that a bit late, but that where the products are matured when you're talking about 6,000 people in technology and hundreds of products, you need a very good management of where you are going to put your investment, where the value is. The portfolio management becomes very important. We use product maturity model for that now to say, our product is mature or not mature, and it can go left and right in the maturity curve.

Sources indicate that location strategy. Most companies, they assume that engineering can be even in-sourced where they are your own teams. They can be in various different locations, but if you're not careful, product management sits somewhere else, engineering sits somewhere else, program sits somewhere else. Try to create self-sufficient teams. I touched on three parts of those transformation, a little bit of each one of them to say what's key. There are many more in that one. The biggest point was the more you step back and think about it, you will avoid costly re-implementation and migration. That's huge. It spends a lot of time and spend of cost.

Final two slides on what are some of the tips if you are following the transformation at scale. Three pillars, we talked about that. Just system transformation is not enough. Change business processes when required, because they are just organically developed like your technology systems as well. Question that to say, is that really different? Why should four different countries have different operational processes? Simplify operation. Build core capabilities, we just talked about that. Because now we have the tech platform which supports this retail platform for those same CI/CDs, the observabilities, everything, but we could have started that early. Start that early. Throughput is a long game. Today also we get a lot of pressures, and can we go live in two months? Can we go live in two weeks? Can we go live in three weeks? We can do that if the platform capabilities are there. Total throughput is much higher today, but the same thing could have taken us six months long back when we had to develop those capabilities.

If we didn't do that, now we can do 10 such things and we would never have done that because we would have just duplicated it. Evolve continuously. We used to be very horizontally laid. I ran entire engineering of Tesco, all the platforms, all this thing, but product management was separate. Now that platforms are matured, we are going more vertical. I still run the platforms because that we cannot divide. The core platform is still there, but the application domain wise now we are creating more partnership between business and people like me within technology. Evolution is necessary. E-commerce is not just enough. Avoid tech for tech. Communicate value early. It's very hard to understand outside technology for sure. What are you all doing, is the frequent question we get. How come you are so many people? What's going on? It has gone less and less now. Even within technology, it's hard to explain what value we have created for the business.

We talked about the cost, IP and vendor lock-in. We are very careful when we are talking about agentic code development. We are very careful as to what kind of IP leakage could happen. Vendor lock-in, we talked about it. Even when we use many of the SaaS solutions, we ask for those protections from data sharing perspective, from IP perspective, so that we keep that edge of differentiation for Tesco. Then last one is technology will keep evolving, but if you have set the right culture, I mean there was blockchain there, public cloud before that, MapReduce systems, now agentic part. It will keep happening, and the pace has increased. If you don't have the right culture, the right talent, and the right level of trust within the organization, it won't work.

#92837. Industry News: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1384 w)

Industry News: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • It has been revealed that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

It has been revealed that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

According to recent reports, FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

Industry observers note that you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

In a recent development, every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the massive matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Industry observers note that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Industry observers note that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

Industry observers note that in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

The decoding kernel reveals up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

In a recent development, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Sources indicate that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Sources indicate that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

It has been revealed that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

It has been revealed that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

In a recent development, work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Recent findings suggest that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

It has been revealed that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Industry observers note that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A major thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses.
  • Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps.
  • A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

Recent findings suggest that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the fresh provider can't replay them.

In a recent development, API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

In a recent development, language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

Xint is reporting that it has discovered a collection of five critical vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server. The worst flaw, it says, would allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The company also reports a local-privilege escalation (LPE) kernel vulnerability, which was introduced in the 4.15 kernel, in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) subsystem. If chained with the NGINX vulnerability, it would allow an attacker to gain root privileges on the host. A kernel patch for this is not yet available.

Industry observers note that xint recommends updating to NGINX 1.31.9, which was just released, and to block the SCTP module on hosts that do not need it until a kernel fix is available. See the mitigations section of their report for more information.

Note: you can avoid this step in the future by logging into your LWN account.

📅 20 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (860 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • Recent findings suggest that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

Recent findings suggest that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

In a recent development, the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Sources indicate that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

Sources indicate that the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

In a recent development, transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

In a recent development, models too massive for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

Sources indicate that the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

Recent findings suggest that TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

Industry observers note that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

Recent findings suggest that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

Industry observers note that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It has been revealed that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Sources indicate that TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch customers. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

It has been revealed that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

Tech Report: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • It has been revealed that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

It has been revealed that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

Recent findings suggest that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Upcoming Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

According to recent reports, after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Recent findings suggest that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

It has been revealed that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

It has been revealed that the table reveals which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

In a recent development, each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

According to recent reports, in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

It has been revealed that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Industry observers note that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

According to recent reports, in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

According to recent reports, the table reveals one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Industry observers note that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

According to recent reports, key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The survey included 2,000 senior executives, split evenly between the United States and Germany.
  • The accompanying release says 74% of respondents reported that information volume can get in the way of decisions, while 75% remarked decisions stall when critical information is not available at the right time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that companies are giving AI a bigger role in decisions, but that does not mean their leaders find decisions easier. In a survey published by Körber, 76% of senior decision-makers said decision-making had become more complex. The same share reported allowing AI to play a greater role. The answers describe two trends happening at the same time; they do not establish that one caused the other.

The survey included 2,000 senior executives, split evenly between the United States and Germany. Körber says respondents worked for organizations with annual revenue above $250 million and at least 250 employees, and fieldwork ran from August 27 to September 8, 2026. That makes the findings a look at decision-making inside larger organizations in two markets, not a representative measure of every employer or of small businesses.

The accompanying release says 74% of respondents reported that information volume can get in the way of decisions, while 75% remarked decisions stall when critical information is not available at the right time. Having more data and having the right data when a decision is due are different problems.

Industry observers note that consider a manager who needs to decide whether to delay a shipment. Sales, warehouse operations and finance may have different records for the same order, all updated at different times. An AI assistant can summarize those records quickly, but a faster summary does not establish which number is current or who can approve an exception. Unless the team can check the sources and resolve conflicting records, the tool can move the work of reconciliation from one person to another rather than eliminate it.

The survey also found that 73% of respondents were uncomfortable letting technology make the final decision. That helps explain why businesses may want AI in the workflow without giving it control of the outcome. Drafting an explanation, gathering supporting documents and making a decision that commits the company are separate jobs. The cost of an error differs for each.

Among respondents whose organizations described their transformation as enterprise-wide, 63.8% reported strong organizational performance, compared with 41.6% of those at the pilot stage. Future-readiness confidence was 66.4% and 46.5%, respectively. Intends to invest significantly in AI decision support were almost identical: 59% for the enterprise-wide group, versus 59.4% for the pilot group.

Sources indicate that those are self-reported group differences, not measured returns from a controlled rollout. Organizations that can implement technology across departments may already have stronger data, more resources or better operating processes. The publication does not establish that expanding a pilot causes performance to improve. It is better read as a prompt to ask what mature implementations do differently and which of those practices a particular team can test.

In a recent development, the practical question for an operator is where a tool improves the work between a question and a decision. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a way to formalize responsibilities and decide what to measure in context. Teams can pick a recurring decision and compare how long it takes to obtain the necessary evidence, how often a recommendation must be corrected and whether an approver can explain what they relied on.

Sources indicate that tracking these measures separately can reveal a trade-off that a single adoption number misses. A tool may produce reports faster while increasing the time spent checking them, or it may let people spend less time gathering facts and more time evaluating options. For the executives surveyed, the challenge is not simply making AI more available. It is defining the role it plays when information is incomplete and someone still has to own the decision.
