📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities.
  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.

According to Meta engineers, modern GPU architectures offer advanced performance-optimization features, including warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution, which depart from Triton's traditional programming model, which simplifies kernel development but abstracts away low-level execution structures.

Industry observers note that for example, a modern FlashAttention kernel may dedicate one warp group to issuing TMA transfers while another executes tensor-core computation. A Blackwell GEMM kernel may coordinate multiple warp groups, TMEM allocations, and cluster resources simultaneously. In both cases, performance depends not only on the computation being performed, but also on how multiple execution agents cooperate.

In a recent development, using these advanced features required "large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code", as they were not readily available as Triton compilers abstractions. To address this challenge, Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to give engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton's programming model.

TLX introduces a newly introduced Multiple Instructions, Multiple Warps (MIMW) execution model that bridges CUDA’s thread-level control and Triton’s block-level abstraction. It extends Triton across five key areas: warp-group orchestration, synchronization, memory orchestration, cluster execution, and optional layout.

Taken together, these capabilities allow TLX to occupy the space between Triton’s productivity and CUDA’s control. Developers retain the advantages of Python, autotuning, and blocked tensor programming while gaining direct access to the execution structures that increasingly determine performance on modern GPUs.

Meta has deployed TLX in production for several months across three major workloads. For GEM model training on thousands of NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, TLX achieved 20–25% end-to-end Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) with up to 2x forward-pass speedup. For In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) in recommendation inference, TLX delivered a 4x speedup on an H100 for a linear compression kernel and reduced compute-intensive net latency up to two-thirds in co-designed models. Finally, in distributed grouped GEMM for LLM pretraining, TLX improved performance, reliability, and maintainability across large GPU fleets for extended training periods.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, AI engineer Kritika Choudary observed:.

When I wrote Flash Attention from scratch in Metal on my M2, the tile loads into threadgroup memory and where to put the barriers were where most of the thinking went, so it's nice to see TLX make that explicit.

On a similar note, Amirul Islam emphasized that:.

Making warp-group handoffs explicit while leaving layouts optional feels like a useful boundary. The producer/consumer pipeline is visible in the source, without forcing every fused stage to start with manual layout bookkeeping.

Meta looks to further expand Triton TLX by adding support for additional NVIDIA, AMD, and custom accelerator architectures, automating warp-group orchestration through higher-level abstractions, and integrating TLX with torch.compile.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Thinking Machines Lab Releases Inkling 2 Mini for Local Devices

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026, an open-weights model built to run on consumer laptops.
  • Recent findings suggest that the full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and a companion research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, are available on Hugging Face.
  • In a recent development, A organization demonstration shows Inkling 2 Mini running offline on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode during a flight, where it built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026, an open-weights model built to run on consumer laptops. It has 26.4 billion total parameters and a memory footprint of about 20GB, using repeated passes through its middle layers to improve reasoning.

Recent findings suggest that the full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and a companion research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, are available on Hugging Face. Tinker offers inference and fine-tuning, with chat in Tinker Playground, while local options include Ollama on Mac systems with at least 32GB of RAM and GGUF versions through Unsloth and llama.cpp.

In a recent development, A organization demonstration shows Inkling 2 Mini running offline on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode during a flight, where it built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes. Another demonstration uses one offline MacBook to power all 20 residents of Thinkyville, a simulated pixel town, illustrating how multiple persistent agents can run locally.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer, meaning only a subset of its specialized components is used for each token. Its 24 layers are divided into four blocks of six. The first and last blocks run once, while the two middle blocks share weights and run three times, producing 48 layer applications per token from 24 stored layers. The model has 3.4 billion active parameters and 5.4 billion weight activations per token once looping is included.

Attention residuals let each layer learn its own mixture of earlier block outputs instead of adding every output into a single running sum. The second and third passes also receive a gated message from the preceding pass. That gate initially blocks the message and learns to admit more of it during training, allowing looping to be introduced without destabilizing the model.

In the tech giant’s training comparison, an unpruned non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512,000-token agentic traces.

According to recent reports, training began with 384 experts and eight selected per token. Two-thirds were pruned during midtraining, leaving the 128 most-used experts in each layer, after which the model trained on 1 trillion tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model to recover its earlier performance. Twenty layers were trained and are deployed in 4-bit NVFP4, with the final four in 8-bit MXFP8; the organization says matching training and deployment precision avoids conversion loss from post-training quantization.

Thinking Machines Lab reports scores of 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 77.9% on the 51-task SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard evaluation, compared with 42.2% and 73.8% for Qwen3.8-27B, respectively, alongside 46.5% on Vals Index v2.2. Its comparison notes that evaluation setups vary by model.

The company states looping improves reasoning without enabling the weights to store more facts; knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s AA-Omniscience result is in line with other models of its size, while its leads among similar-sized open-weights models on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA and MCP Atlas come from efficient use of search and tools.

It has been revealed that the company also says Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or instructions with many constraints, reporting 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1. It trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks including CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

It has been revealed that looping complicates chain-of-thought monitoring, the practice of reading a model’s written reasoning to oversee its behavior. A conventional transformer must externalize reasoning that needs additional sequential steps; a looped model can perform more of those steps internally before producing text. Reasoning that never enters the text cannot be inspected by that kind of monitor.

Because Inkling 2 Mini supports only a fixed number of passes, the lab trained TML-d24-varloop-research with one to five passes, mostly three, and conducted reinforcement learning at three. On a Think Fast subset, the company reports that its no-chain-of-thought time horizon, defined as the human completion time of tasks it can finish at 50% reliability without written reasoning, rose from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three before roughly flattening. N-Hop Lookup accuracy continued improving through ten loops even though training had not exceeded five passes.

Sources indicate that in the company’s initial analysis of GPQA Diamond questions answered correctly at every tested depth, average reasoning traces fell from 3,703 tokens at one pass to 1,661 at five. Mean sentence length changed only from 8.9 to 8.7 words, and the share of words found in an English dictionary moved from 94.6% to 94.4%; the shorter traces were more direct and involved less backtracking.

Sources indicate that the agentic tests used a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-loop model in LinuxArena. With Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as a weaker monitor, the firm found no clear trend in stealth rate as loop count increased; restricting the monitor to tool calls and outputs left a significant number of attacks undetected.

These monitorability results are preliminary. Reinforcement learning only at three passes means the experiments do not establish what a model trained at higher pass counts would learn, and the manufacturer cautions that such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively.

Industry observers note that for oversight researchers, the open question is whether the legibility observed at this scale survives larger models and training regimes that optimize deeper loops. The fixed and variable open-weights releases provide a direct way to investigate that question across looping depths.

  • Sources indicate that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

According to recent reports, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Sources indicate that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

According to recent reports, the integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

According to recent reports, our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

According to recent reports, model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

According to recent reports, transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

It has been revealed that A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

In a recent development, one detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

Sources indicate that the first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

It has been revealed that we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

In a recent development, the Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Industry observers note that our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

According to recent reports, we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Industry observers note that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

Recent findings suggest that so we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Industry observers note that coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

  • US Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff are examining potential accounting challenges at NVIDIA, according to two people briefed on the matter, Reuters reported on November 20, 2026.
  • According to recent reports, the Wall Street Journal reported the investigation’s existence on November 17, 2026, but mentioned it could not determine its focus.
  • An SEC spokesperson declined to comment, and NVIDIA spokespeople did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff are examining potential accounting challenges at NVIDIA, according to two people briefed on the matter, Reuters reported on November 20, 2026. NVIDIA shares were down about 13% after the report, having fallen more than 6% beforehand, according to LSEG data.

According to recent reports, the Wall Street Journal reported the investigation’s existence on November 17, 2026, but mentioned it could not determine its focus. The people spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential complications.

An SEC spokesperson declined to comment, and NVIDIA spokespeople did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The report leaves the inquiry’s opening date and precise accounting questions unresolved. An investigation is not evidence of wrongdoing, and many close without enforcement action.

In a recent development, the disclosure followed NVIDIA’s November 17 earnings release, which reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter ended October 25, 2026, up 103% year over year, including $107.6 billion from Data Center. Its quarter-end balance sheet listed $81.0 billion in net accounts receivable, $44.2 billion in marketable equity securities and $65.5 billion in non-marketable securities. The cash-flow statement reported $15.7 billion of equity-security purchases during the quarter. Those figures show the scale of NVIDIA’s financial reporting and investment activity, but none has been identified as a subject of the SEC inquiry.

Public scrutiny has also focused on NVIDIA’s geographic revenue presentation and its financing relationships across the AI industry, though neither has been identified as a subject of the investigation. NVIDIA previously changed its geographic reporting to use customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, saying this better reflected the geographic profile of its revenue. The change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown.

Recent findings suggest that analysts and investors have also raised concerns about circular AI financing, in which chipmakers use complex financial arrangements to help customers fund chip purchases and data-center construction. NVIDIA has backed AI companies and cloud providers and provided guarantees connected to data-center projects using its equipment. Critics say these arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess the quality of chipmakers’ revenue and their true financial exposure.

On the November 17 earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress noted NVIDIA was proud of its role supporting the AI industry but would be far more selective about future AI industry financing deals.

SEC Division of Enforcement Director David Woodcock told Reuters in October 2026 that the agency was examining AI companies’ corporate disclosures to ensure issuers give investors a full picture of potential risks.

Separately, the SEC revealed on August 5, 2026 that it was establishing a Financial Reporting and Accounting Unit within its Division of Enforcement. Staffed by specialized attorneys and accountants, the unit is tasked with pursuing financial-reporting fraud and misconduct in accounting and auditing.

In prepared remarks on September 18, 2026, Woodcock described financial reporting and internal accounting controls as central enforcement priorities. He said financial-reporting cases are among the division’s most challenging and lengthy, often taking several years from opening to charging, and that the unit would bring dedicated expertise and a more consistent approach to those cases.

For now, the disclosure sharpens the regulatory question around NVIDIA without answering it. The specific accounting practices under review remain unidentified, and Woodcock’s warning about the length of financial-reporting cases makes the investigation’s duration a central part of its potential impact on the company.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities.
  • It has been revealed that our goal is to be exhaustive.
  • As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

It has been revealed that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Sources indicate that results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where upcoming models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Recent findings suggest that every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

  • The research by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis concerns models of weather, climate, turbulence and other nonlinear processes.
  • It has been revealed that chaotic systems are highly sensitive to initial conditions, so tiny differences can produce dramatically different outcomes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MIT researchers have developed a machine-learning framework that guarantees bounded trajectories for AI models of chaotic systems, addressing simulations that can drift into physically impossible values during long runs. MIT revealed the work on November 20, 2026.

The research by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis concerns models of weather, climate, turbulence and other nonlinear processes. Their paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences was published online on October 12, 2026, and appeared in the journal’s October 20, 2026, matter.

It has been revealed that chaotic systems are highly sensitive to initial conditions, so tiny differences can produce dramatically different outcomes. A neural network may match data over a short period and still fail when left to run: small errors can accumulate until its simulated values grow without limit, even though the real system remains bounded. That behavior can invalidate estimates of long-term statistics, a central goal of modeling dissipative chaotic systems.

In a recent development, the guarantee therefore concerns long-term bounded behavior rather than exact point-by-point forecasting far into the future. It seeks to preserve valid long-run statistics without suppressing the complicated variation that makes the system chaotic. As Azizan put it, “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.”.

The framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator, which predicts how the system evolves, and an energy-like representation. That representation is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint inside a projection layer, which adjusts the model’s predicted evolution. Outside a learned boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, drawing trajectories toward the bounded region while allowing chaotic behavior within it.

Industry observers note that the paper says this construction enforces dissipation by design and provides formal trajectory-boundedness guarantees over arbitrarily long forecast windows. The learned energy boundary also supplies an outer estimate of the system’s strange attractor, whose complex geometry makes it difficult to characterize directly.

Tang noted soft penalties or incentives applied during training need not hold when a deployed model faces new inputs, so unbounded predictions remain possible. Arbitrary caps can keep outputs within a chosen limit, but they can also restrict the model’s ability to represent complex features that should be learned from data. The projection layer is modular and model-agnostic, allowing it to work with different neural-network architectures.

MIT reports that the approach closely tracked true outcomes in tests ranging from textbook systems to complex multidimensional cases, while conventional methods moved into impossible predictions. The published demonstrations include Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, where the method produced bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserved invariant statistics.

It has been revealed that A related Energy-Constrained Operator paper by Andrea Goertzen, Tang and Azizan was published on June 7, 2026. It introduced a closed-form quadratic projection layer and reported stable long-horizon forecasts that captured invariant statistics for systems governed by the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky and Navier–Stokes equations. Both papers use control-theoretic energy conditions to tackle predictions whose unbounded growth prevents meaningful evaluation of long-run statistics.

The algorithms and computer code have been deposited on GitHub, and the paper and open-source code are accessible online. The researchers hope other teams will build on the modular layer and test it on larger, more complex problems.

In a recent development, the team prepares to test progressively larger systems and data-driven models of realistic weather. Realistic-weather performance therefore remains an open research question: the immediate contribution is a formal limit on runaway simulations, while the next tests must establish how that guarantee affects the usefulness of models’ long-term statistics.

#92772. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1737 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
  • Industry observers note that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
  • Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Industry observers note that both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

Sources indicate that it lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Recent findings suggest that nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

According to recent reports, there's no public corpus of intends, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

Industry observers note that "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

The coder reasons about geometry:.

Industry observers note that "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

According to recent reports, the teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

According to recent reports, the hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

According to recent reports, what fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Sources indicate that users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the initiative and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

It has been revealed that the model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Sources indicate that figure 1. An illustration of the same initiative without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

Recent findings suggest that first, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

Sources indicate that we evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a blueprint, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

It has been revealed that figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

It has been revealed that palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

Recent findings suggest that presentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

Sources indicate that we also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1286 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
  • According to recent reports, in April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms.
  • It has been revealed that OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

According to recent reports, in April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

It has been revealed that OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

Sources indicate that however, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

In a recent development, run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that rapidly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Sources indicate that say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:.

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

In a recent development, either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

Sources indicate that the base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:.

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Sources indicate that cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

It has been revealed that this is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

According to recent reports, SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

Recent findings suggest that on a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Nov 21, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that grafana Labs has released Grafana 13.3 with cross-dashboard variables that let teams manage shared dashboard controls in one place. The release also introduces Notebooks for collecting panels and investigation notes in a document that colleagues can share.

In a recent development, the release announcement describes cross-dashboard variables as a public preview across all Grafana editions. Teams can define a variable once and use it in multiple dashboards, avoiding separate configurations for a selector such as an environment or a region. Grafana claims managing those copies separately can lead to configuration drift.

Cross-dashboard variables address a longstanding user request. In a 2021 GitHub discussion, Grafana user Darth-Bobo described having to maintain the same variables separately across dashboards, warning that configuration differences could become "unmanageable over time". More recently, an early tester described shared variables as useful for evaluating Git Sync without Terraform templating.

Variables can have global scope, which makes them available throughout a Grafana organisation, or folder scope, which limits them to dashboards in the same folder. An editor can add the available variables from a dashboard sidebar, either individually or all at once. Viewers can still change the selected value on a dashboard, while the variable configuration remains centrally managed.

According to recent reports, teams running Grafana themselves must enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle to try the preview. Grafana places the management screen under Dashboards > Variables, separate from the dashboard editor where customers add the shared controls.

Notebooks are also in public preview across all editions. A notebook can hold panels from dashboards or Explore alongside written observations, with findings from Grafana Assistant included as well. Teams can use the document to record how they investigated an matter or to prepare a post-incident review with relevant panels already in place.

Industry observers note that users can create a notebook manually or through Grafana Assistant, then save and share it. Grafana is rolling the feature out gradually to Grafana Cloud. Self-managed installations need the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle enabled.

According to recent reports, grafana’s Notebooks joins similar investigation-document workflows from other observability vendors. Datadog Notebooks combines live graphs with rich text and supports simultaneous editing, inline comments and reusable postmortem templates. New Relic Notebooks, generally available since August 2026, combines NRQL queries, visualisations and Markdown, with natural-language query translation and notebook-wide variables.

Recent findings suggest that the release also changes how Grafana Assistant builds dashboards. In public preview, dashboard looks let a user describe what they want to monitor and review a proposed layout in chat before building it. The plan covers the title and the proposed panels, including visualisation types and variables. A read-only preview lets the user refine the plan before choosing to build and save the dashboard.

Industry observers note that A separate Assistant feature, Undo turn, is generally available across all editions. It restores the previous dashboard state after an Assistant edit, including when one request changed multiple panels. The Assistant dashboarding guide notes that undo is unavailable if the dashboard has changed since the Assistant's edit.

Industry observers note that grafana 13.3 also previews a visual refresh with revised themes and interface components. Grafana Labs claims the visual refresh preserves existing navigation and workflows and introduces no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins using standard Grafana components and theme tokens pick up the new appearance; those with custom styling can migrate separately. Self-managed customers can enable grafana.visualDesignRefresh to try it and switch back to the previous design.

Bloomberg reported on November 20, 2026, that CrowdStrike was in ongoing talks to acquire Zscaler, citing people familiar with the matter, in a report carried by CNBC. Zscaler shares rose 18% in extended trading following the report, while CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.

No acquisition agreement has been unveiled. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report, and Zscaler did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

CNBC put CrowdStrike’s market capitalization at $235 billion after its stock roughly doubled during 2026, while Zscaler’s was about $32 billion after a 13% decline during the year.

A completed transaction would rank among cybersecurity’s largest, CNBC noted. Its comparisons were Google’s $32 billion acquisition of Wiz in 2025, Cisco’s roughly $28 billion purchase of Splunk in 2024 and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk in 2026.

According to recent reports, zscaler’s September 2, 2026 partnership announcement details an existing technical relationship between the companies. The expanded partnership is intended to automate security workflows and support real-time, adaptive Zero Trust enforcement by connecting CrowdStrike’s detection and response with Zscaler’s access controls.

Industry observers note that zscaler said a planned integration using the OpenID Shared Signals Framework, an industry-standard method for sharing risk context, would let Falcon continuously evaluate user risk and pass that context to Zscaler’s Adaptive Access Engine. When suspicious endpoint behavior is detected, Zscaler can then automatically adjust access to match the current risk posture.

Sources indicate that the companies are also developing a native Falcon Foundry application built on Zscaler OneAPI. Planned functions include triggering Zscaler enforcement from Charlotte Agentic SOAR, CrowdStrike’s security automation interface, and supporting end-to-end automated remediation without middleware, connectors or separate infrastructure.

According to recent reports, zscaler said network-event and AI-event logs are designed to stream into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, CrowdStrike’s security-event management platform, where they can be correlated with Falcon endpoint, identity and cloud data. The combined telemetry is designed to help analysts reconstruct multi-stage attacks across domains. The AI telemetry includes AI-application interactions, risky chatbot prompts and policy violations, placing AI-specific risks alongside network and user activity in a unified investigation interface.

Under the partnership strategy, CrowdStrike would also expand Project QuiltWorks, an industry coalition focused on frontier AI risk, to include Zscaler. Zscaler cautioned that unreleased services and features covered by the announcement remained in development and subject to change.

On November 3, 2026, CrowdStrike announced a definitive agreement to acquire Fiddler AI to add pre-deployment evaluation, continuous agent observability and explainability to Falcon. A separate agreement to acquire Dreadnode would add automated pre-deployment security testing of AI models, applications and agents. Both proposed acquisitions were expected to close in CrowdStrike’s fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.

Recent findings suggest that the reported talks sit on top of an existing integration roadmap rather than a relationship built from scratch. The open question is whether that roadmap remains a partner integration or becomes part of a single tech giant; for now, the documented product work and the reported transaction are at different stages, with several of the partnership’s features still in development.

#92759. Latest Update: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1373 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • Sources indicate that we've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

Sources indicate that we've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

Recent findings suggest that we confirmed Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early consumers. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created fresh challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

In a recent development, it runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

Sources indicate that the launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

Sources indicate that we built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It has been revealed that it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Sources indicate that phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

Recent findings suggest that the prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a newly introduced one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

It has been revealed that we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

It has been revealed that phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

It has been revealed that congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly demonstrates where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

AWS Routes HyperPod Inference Across Regions From One Endpoint

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AWS introduced Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway on November 20, 2026, giving customers one managed endpoint for inference requests across registered HyperPod clusters in a single AWS Region or multiple Regions.
  • Recent findings suggest that the launch adds a second routing tier above the existing SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway.
  • In a recent development, AWS is addressing a capacity-utilization problem: requests can queue on a saturated cluster while already-provisioned GPUs sit idle elsewhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AWS introduced Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway on November 20, 2026, giving customers one managed endpoint for inference requests across registered HyperPod clusters in a single AWS Region or multiple Regions. The service selects a cluster using capacity, queue, proximity and error signals, with automatic failover when a cluster becomes unavailable.

Recent findings suggest that the launch adds a second routing tier above the existing SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway. That cluster-level gateway continues to select individual model pods using signals including key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth; the upcoming global tier selects the cluster first, while leaving pod selection unchanged.

In a recent development, AWS is addressing a capacity-utilization problem: requests can queue on a saturated cluster while already-provisioned GPUs sit idle elsewhere. In its example of four models served across five clusters in two Regions, per-model serving requires clients to track 20 endpoints. Cluster-level gateways cut that to five, while the global gateway provides one. The managed tier removes the need to build and maintain load balancers, DNS and cross-Region networking for this routing, and lets peak traffic overflow to clusters with available capacity.

Sources indicate that an operator publishes each participating cluster by enabling spec.globalRouting in its existing InferenceGatewayConfig, then calls CreateGlobalInferenceGateway with the clusters to group. Publishing creates a Network Load Balancer, a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint service and certificate resources in the customer’s account. An unpublished cluster cannot be added successfully.

Clients send OpenAI-compatible requests signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) to the regional endpoint. The gateway authenticates the caller and selects a healthy cluster, AWS PrivateLink carries the request within or across Regions, and the cluster’s Inference Gateway chooses the model pod. SageMaker operates the routing fleet, private endpoints, certificate validation, health checks, authentication and rate limiting; a service-managed publisher on each cluster supplies load metrics.

For each request, the gateway scores healthy clusters using four configurable signals:.

Customers overriding the defaults must set all four weights, using values from 0.0 to 1.0 that total 1.0, and can disable a signal with zero. UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway changes the weighting for latest requests without reprovisioning, while in-flight requests finish under the old settings. AWS indicates workloads that prioritize resilience over proximity can raise ErrorRate and lower RegionProximity.

In a recent development, the gateway health-checks every cluster and shifts traffic to the next-best cluster after a failure without requiring client changes, bringing a recovered cluster back gradually. A failed request is retried once on another cluster unless streaming has started; if no healthy cluster remains, the gateway returns HTTP 503. Adding a healthy cluster does not change the endpoint or disrupt other clusters, while removing one stops new requests but lets in-flight work finish.

IAM separately controls standard and streaming invocation, and customer JSON Web Tokens, when used, travel inside the SigV4 signature. Requests reach clusters only over AWS PrivateLink, and AWS states that the gateway does not log or store prompts or completions. Deleting the global gateway stops its endpoint but leaves the per-cluster endpoints serving.

It has been revealed that bagelcode VP of AI Platform Jinhyung Park noted in AWS’s announcement that beta tests routed requests across two Regions through the gateway and continued serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave the firm’s small platform team cross-Region failover without building or maintaining its own routing layer.

According to recent reports, the service is available in 13 Regions: US East (N. Virginia and Ohio), US West (N. California and Oregon), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London and Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo, Mumbai, Singapore and Sydney).

AWS advises single-cluster customers to remain on the cluster Inference Gateway endpoint and adopt the global service when adding a second cluster. Existing per-cluster endpoints continue serving during client migration, and a gateway containing only clusters in one Region can keep a workload there. A published cluster left outside any gateway receives no traffic even though its Network Load Balancer continues to run and incur charges.

By putting proximity, capacity and failure signals in one policy, the service makes the use of otherwise idle GPU capacity a configuration decision rather than a separate networking project.

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1962 w)
